title: What you will be able to do
instruction: Press reveal to see each outcome for this lesson.

_items.text: Read a journal article strategically by its structure, rather than reading it start to finish.

title: Reading an article is not reading a story
body: A journal article is not written to be read from the first word to the last. It has a structure, and knowing that structure lets you decide what to read first, and what you can skip.

title: The book's own structure
body: Dennis and Abbott (2026, pp.121-123) set out the sections of a journal article in the order a reader meets them, in their Table 8.1, and then apply that structure to a worked example. The sections generally run from abstract through introduction, method, results, and discussion to conclusion, but the order you should read them in is not the order they are printed in.

title: Worked example
body:
Consider two students who have each been given the same journal article to use.

{{learner-a}} starts at the introduction and reads straight through to the conclusion, in print order.

{{learner-b}} reads the abstract and conclusion first, then the method, and only turns to the introduction if they still need the background.

Both finished the article. Only {{learner-b}} had decided how to read it, rather than simply starting at the top.

title: Why method-first is a critical choice
body: Reading the method before the discussion means you judge the findings on how they were produced, not just on how convincingly they are described afterwards. That order is a critical decision, not a shortcut.

displayTitle: Four things worth checking in a method section
body: The method section is where a study's claim is actually tested.
instruction: Select each tab to see what to check for.

_items.title: Sample
_items.body: Who or what was studied, and how many. A claim about a wide population needs a sample that could support it.

_items.title: Design
_items.body: How the study was set up. A comparison needs something to compare against, not just a single group observed once.

_items.title: Measures
_items.body: What was actually measured, and whether that measure really captures the thing the claim is about.

_items.title: Limitations
_items.body: What the authors themselves admit the study cannot show. This is often the most honest part of the method section.

title: Reading route checklist
body: Use this order when you next read a journal article for a task.
instruction: Tick each item once you have tried it.

_items.text: Did I read the abstract and conclusion before anything else?
Did I check the method before reading the discussion?
Did I note the sample size and design before judging the finding?
Did I only read the introduction once I knew I needed the background?

title: Making this your default
body: Try this reading order on the next article you are given, even if nobody asks you to. Abstract and conclusion first, then method, then decide if you need the introduction. It takes the same time overall, but you judge the claim rather than just absorbing it.

title: Your turn
instruction: This is for your own reflection; no right answers are expected.

_items.text: Think of an article you read recently start to finish. What would you have noticed sooner by reading the method first?
Is there a habit from this lesson you could apply to the very next article you are given?
